question: Under the federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act (Title X), the lead-based paint disclosure requirements apply to housing built before what year?
explanation: Title X and its implementing EPA/HUD regulation (40 CFR Part 745) apply to "target housing," defined as housing built before 1978, the year the federal government banned consumer uses of lead-based paint.
source_note: Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992 (Title X of the Housing and Community Development Act); 40 CFR Part 745

question: In a sale of pre-1978 housing, federal law gives buyers how many days, unless a different period is mutually agreed upon in writing, to conduct a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment before becoming obligated under the contract?
choice_a: 3 days
choice_b: 5 days
choice_c: 10 days
choice_d: 30 days
explanation: The federal lead-based paint disclosure rule gives purchasers a 10-day period (which the parties may lengthen, shorten, or waive in writing) to conduct a paint inspection or risk assessment for lead-based paint hazards before they are obligated under the purchase contract.
source_note: 40 CFR 745.110 / 24 CFR 35.88 (EPA/HUD Lead Disclosure Rule)

question: Which document must a seller or landlord of pre-1978 housing give to a buyer or tenant as part of the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements?
choice_a: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment report
choice_b: A FEMA flood insurance rate map
choice_c: A Comprehensive Environmental Response Cost Statement
choice_d: The EPA pamphlet "Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home"
explanation: Federal regulations require sellers and lessors of target housing to provide purchasers and tenants with the EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet, "Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home," along with any known lead-based paint disclosures.
source_note: 40 CFR 745.107 (EPA/HUD Lead Disclosure Rule)

question: A licensee is helping a buyer purchase a home built in 1965. What is the licensee's obligation regarding lead-based paint?
choice_a: The licensee must ensure the seller discloses known lead-based paint/hazard information and provides the required EPA pamphlet, since the home qualifies as "target housing"
choice_b: No disclosure obligation exists because the home predates modern environmental laws
choice_c: The licensee must personally test the property for lead before listing it
choice_d: Disclosure is only required if the buyer specifically asks about lead paint
explanation: Because the home was built before 1978, it is "target housing" under the federal lead disclosure rule. Agents are responsible for ensuring their clients comply with the disclosure and pamphlet-delivery requirements, even though the agent is not required to test for lead themselves.
source_note: 40 CFR Part 745; EPA/HUD Real Estate Disclosure Rule guidance for agents

question: What is the EPA's recommended action level for radon gas in indoor air, above which mitigation is generally advised?
choice_a: 0.4 pCi/L
choice_b: 4 pCi/L
choice_c: 40 pCi/L
choice_d: 400 pCi/L
explanation: The EPA recommends that homes be fixed if a radon test shows a level of 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) of air or higher, and homeowners should consider fixing between 2 and 4 pCi/L as well.
source_note: EPA "A Citizen's Guide to Radon"

question: Which statement about asbestos in older buildings is most accurate?
choice_a: Asbestos must always be removed immediately when found in any structure
choice_b: Asbestos was never used in residential construction
choice_c: Asbestos-containing materials pose the greatest health risk when they are friable (easily crumbled) and fibers become airborne
choice_d: Federal law requires every home seller to test for asbestos before closing
explanation: Asbestos is most hazardous when it is friable or disturbed (e.g., during renovation or demolition), releasing fibers into the air that can be inhaled. Intact, non-friable asbestos-containing material is often left in place and managed rather than automatically removed, and there is no blanket federal pre-sale testing mandate for residential asbestos.
source_note: EPA asbestos guidance; Clean Air Act NESHAP for asbestos (40 CFR Part 61, Subpart M)

question: Under the Clean Air Act's National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP), what is generally required before renovation or demolition of a building that may contain asbestos?
choice_a: Nothing, since NESHAP only applies to industrial smokestacks
choice_b: Automatic condemnation of the property
choice_c: A Phase II Environmental Site Assessment only
choice_d: An asbestos inspection and, where applicable, notification to the appropriate regulatory agency before work begins
explanation: The asbestos NESHAP under the Clean Air Act requires an inspection for asbestos-containing material before renovation or demolition and imposes work practice and notification requirements to control emissions of asbestos fibers.
source_note: Clean Air Act; 40 CFR Part 61, Subpart M (Asbestos NESHAP)

question: Which statement best describes the current federal regulatory status of mold in residential property?
choice_a: There is no federal regulatory standard specifically limiting mold in homes; the EPA provides guidance, but disclosure and remediation are generally governed by state/local law and general disclosure duties
choice_b: The EPA has established a legally enforceable federal action level for mold spore counts in homes
choice_c: Mold is regulated exclusively under CERCLA as a hazardous substance
choice_d: All mold must be remediated under the Clean Water Act before a property can be sold
explanation: Unlike lead-based paint, there is no federal law setting numeric limits for mold in indoor air or requiring specific mold disclosures. The EPA publishes guidance on moisture and mold control, but any disclosure obligations for known mold problems arise from general state disclosure law and common-law duties, not a specific federal mold statute.
source_note: EPA "Mold Remediation in Schools and Commercial Buildings" guidance; absence of federal mold statute

question: Leaking underground storage tanks (USTs) are a common cause of which environmental problem affecting real property?
choice_a: Wetlands destruction
choice_b: Groundwater contamination
choice_c: Urban heat islands
choice_d: Ozone depletion
explanation: Leaking underground storage tanks, historically used to store petroleum products and other regulated substances, are a leading cause of soil and groundwater contamination, which is why EPA administers a dedicated UST program.
source_note: EPA Underground Storage Tank (UST) program; RCRA Subtitle I

question: Underground storage tanks are primarily regulated at the federal level under which statute?
choice_a: The Clean Water Act
choice_b: The Fair Housing Act
choice_c: Subtitle I of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA)
choice_d: The Endangered Species Act
explanation: Congress added Subtitle I to RCRA in 1984 to establish a comprehensive federal program regulating underground storage tanks, including technical standards, leak detection, and financial responsibility requirements for tank owners/operators.
source_note: RCRA Subtitle I (added by the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments of 1984); EPA UST program

question: What is a "brownfield" in the context of real estate and environmental law?
choice_a: A federally designated wilderness area protected from all development
choice_b: A newly constructed subdivision built on previously undeveloped farmland
choice_c: Any property located within a FEMA-designated flood zone
choice_d: A property where redevelopment or reuse may be complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant
explanation: A brownfield is real property whose expansion, redevelopment, or reuse may be complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant. Federal brownfields programs provide funding and liability relief to encourage cleanup and reuse of such sites.
source_note: Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act of 2002; EPA Brownfields Program

question: A lender is originating a federally related mortgage loan on a home located in a FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). What is generally required as a result?
choice_a: The lender must require the borrower to obtain flood insurance for the life of the loan
choice_b: The lender must deny the loan application
choice_c: The property must be rezoned as non-residential
choice_d: No special requirement applies unless the buyer requests it
explanation: Under the National Flood Insurance Program framework, federally regulated or federally related lenders must require flood insurance as a condition of a mortgage loan on improved real estate located in a Special Flood Hazard Area shown on FEMA flood maps.
source_note: National Flood Insurance Act; Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973 (as amended); FEMA/NFIP lender requirements

question: Which federal agency's maps are used to determine whether a property lies within a Special Flood Hazard Area for purposes of the National Flood Insurance Program?
choice_a: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
choice_b: The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)
choice_c: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
choice_d: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
explanation: FEMA publishes Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs) that delineate Special Flood Hazard Areas and other flood zones, which lenders and insurers use to determine flood insurance requirements and rates under the National Flood Insurance Program.
source_note: FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs); National Flood Insurance Program

question: Which federal law gives the Army Corps of Engineers and the EPA joint authority to regulate the discharge of dredged or fill material into wetlands and other "waters of the United States"?
choice_a: The Clean Air Act
choice_b: CERCLA
choice_c: Section 404 of the Clean Water Act
choice_d: The Safe Drinking Water Act
explanation: Section 404 of the Clean Water Act establishes a permit program, jointly administered by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the EPA, regulating the discharge of dredged or fill material into wetlands and other waters of the United States, making it central to wetlands protection in real estate development.
source_note: Clean Water Act Section 404 (33 U.S.C. 1344)

question: A developer wants to fill a portion of a wetland to build a parking lot. Before proceeding, the developer most likely needs to obtain a permit from which entity?
choice_a: The local homeowners association
choice_b: The Federal Housing Administration
choice_c: The state department of motor vehicles
choice_d: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, under the Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting program
explanation: Filling or dredging a wetland generally requires a Section 404 permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which coordinates with the EPA in administering the Clean Water Act's wetlands protection program. Developing without a required permit can expose the developer to federal enforcement action.
source_note: Clean Water Act Section 404; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers regulatory program

question: What is the primary purpose of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA), commonly known as "Superfund"?
choice_a: To fund and enable the cleanup of sites contaminated with hazardous substances and to hold responsible parties liable for cleanup costs
choice_b: To set fuel efficiency standards for automobiles
choice_c: To regulate residential lead-based paint disclosures
choice_d: To establish national ambient air quality standards
explanation: CERCLA, enacted in 1980, created a federal program (funded in part by a trust fund, the "Superfund") to identify and clean up sites contaminated with hazardous substances and to impose liability for cleanup costs on potentially responsible parties.
source_note: Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9601 et seq.)

question: Under CERCLA, liability for cleanup costs at a contaminated site can generally be imposed on a current property owner even if that owner did not cause or contribute to the contamination. This type of liability is best described as:
choice_a: Liability requiring proof of negligence
choice_b: Strict, and potentially joint and several, liability that can apply retroactively
choice_c: Liability that only applies to the original polluter, never to subsequent owners
choice_d: Criminal liability only, with no civil cleanup cost exposure
explanation: CERCLA imposes strict liability on potentially responsible parties (PRPs), including current owners/operators, prior owners/operators at the time of disposal, generators, and transporters, without regard to fault. Liability can also be joint and several among multiple PRPs and applies retroactively to contamination that occurred before CERCLA was enacted, which is why environmental due diligence is critical before purchasing commercial or industrial property.
source_note: CERCLA Section 107 (42 U.S.C. 9607); EPA potentially responsible party (PRP) liability framework

question: What did the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA) of 1986 add to the original CERCLA framework?
choice_a: It eliminated all liability for property owners under CERCLA
choice_b: It created the National Flood Insurance Program
choice_c: It reauthorized and strengthened Superfund, increased cleanup funding, and added community right-to-know provisions along with an innocent landowner defense
choice_d: It established the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule
explanation: SARA reauthorized CERCLA, increased Superfund's funding and cleanup requirements, and added the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (EPCRA) provisions, as well as clarifying an innocent landowner defense for purchasers who conducted appropriate due diligence and did not know of contamination at the time of purchase.
source_note: Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986 (SARA)

question: A buyer wants to preserve a potential "innocent landowner" or "bona fide prospective purchaser" defense to CERCLA liability before purchasing a commercial property with a history of industrial use. What should the buyer do before closing?
choice_a: Nothing; the defense applies automatically to all purchasers
choice_b: Wait until after closing to investigate, since pre-purchase inspections void the defense
choice_c: Obtain a homeowner's insurance policy only
choice_d: Conduct "all appropriate inquiries," typically through a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, before acquiring the property
explanation: To qualify for CERCLA's innocent landowner or bona fide prospective purchaser liability protections, a purchaser generally must conduct "all appropriate inquiries" into the prior ownership and uses of the property before acquisition, most commonly satisfied by a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment meeting the ASTM E1527 standard.
source_note: CERCLA innocent landowner defense (42 U.S.C. 9601(35)); Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act of 2002 (bona fide prospective purchaser); ASTM E1527 Phase I ESA standard

question: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) typically includes all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: Collection and laboratory testing of soil and groundwater samples
choice_b: A review of historical property records and prior land uses
choice_c: A visual site inspection for evidence of recognized environmental conditions
choice_d: Interviews with current and past owners or operators
explanation: A Phase I ESA is a non-invasive investigation involving records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews to identify recognized environmental conditions; it does not include sampling or laboratory testing. If a Phase I ESA identifies a recognized environmental condition, a Phase II ESA involving actual sampling and testing is typically the next step.
source_note: ASTM E1527 Standard Practice for Phase I Environmental Site Assessments

question: What distinguishes a Phase II Environmental Site Assessment from a Phase I assessment?
choice_a: Phase II is required before every real estate closing regardless of Phase I findings
choice_b: Phase II involves actual sampling and laboratory testing of soil, water, or air, typically conducted after Phase I identifies a recognized environmental condition
choice_c: Phase II only reviews historical aerial photographs
choice_d: Phase II is performed exclusively by real estate licensees
explanation: A Phase II ESA is triggered when a Phase I assessment identifies a recognized environmental condition warranting further investigation. Unlike Phase I, Phase II involves physical sampling of soil, groundwater, or other media and laboratory analysis to confirm and characterize contamination.
source_note: ASTM E1903 Standard Practice for Phase II Environmental Site Assessments

question: The most heavily contaminated sites identified under CERCLA, which are eligible for federally funded, long-term cleanup, are placed on which list?
choice_a: The Multiple Listing Service (MLS)
choice_b: The National Register of Historic Places
choice_c: The National Priorities List (NPL)
choice_d: The Endangered Species List
explanation: EPA maintains the National Priorities List (NPL) under CERCLA to identify the most seriously contaminated sites in the country that are priorities for long-term, federally funded remedial cleanup action.
source_note: CERCLA; EPA National Priorities List (40 CFR Part 300, Appendix B)

question: Which federal law establishes national air quality standards and, through its asbestos-related provisions, most directly affects real estate transactions involving older buildings undergoing renovation or demolition?
choice_a: The Fair Housing Act
choice_b: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
choice_c: The Truth in Lending Act
choice_d: The Clean Air Act
explanation: The Clean Air Act establishes national ambient air quality standards and, through its NESHAP asbestos regulations, imposes inspection and work-practice requirements before renovating or demolishing structures that may contain asbestos, directly affecting real estate redevelopment projects.
source_note: Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7401 et seq.); 40 CFR Part 61, Subpart M

question: A property's drinking water comes from a private well near an old industrial site. Concerns about contaminants entering the water supply are most directly addressed by which federal statutory scheme?
choice_a: The Clean Water Act and related groundwater protection programs, along with CERCLA where hazardous substances are involved
choice_b: The Fair Housing Act
choice_c: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
choice_d: The Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
explanation: Federal water quality and groundwater contamination concerns are primarily addressed through the Clean Water Act (surface water and wetlands) and, where hazardous substances from an industrial site are the source, CERCLA cleanup authority; neither the Fair Housing Act, RESPA, nor the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act governs environmental contamination.
source_note: Clean Water Act; CERCLA groundwater contamination provisions

question: A large federal highway project is proposed near a residential subdivision. Before the project can proceed, federal law requires an evaluation of significant environmental effects. This requirement stems from which law?
choice_a: The Fair Housing Act
choice_b: The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which requires environmental impact statements for major federal actions
choice_c: RESPA
choice_d: The Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
explanation: The National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) assessing the environmental effects of proposed major federal actions, such as federally funded highway projects, before they proceed.
source_note: National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.

question: A seller is selling a home "as-is" and knows the property has a serious, non-obvious environmental hazard, such as a failing underground heating oil tank that has leaked. Which statement is most accurate regarding the seller's disclosure duty?
choice_a: An "as-is" clause automatically relieves the seller of any duty to disclose known material defects, including environmental hazards
choice_b: Disclosure is only required if the buyer's lender specifically demands it
choice_c: Selling "as-is" generally does not eliminate the seller's duty to disclose known material facts or defects, including known environmental hazards, that a buyer would not readily discover
choice_d: The seller has no disclosure duty because environmental issues are solely the buyer's responsibility to investigate
explanation: In most jurisdictions, an "as-is" clause affects the seller's obligation to repair or the buyer's ability to negotiate over condition, but it does not eliminate the seller's independent duty to affirmatively disclose known material defects or hazards, particularly latent ones like a leaking underground tank, that materially affect value or desirability.
source_note: General real estate disclosure law principles; common-law duty to disclose known material latent defects

question: A listing agent learns from the seller that a portion of the backyard was once used to dispose of chemical waste from a former on-site business, though the area now looks like ordinary lawn. What is the agent's best course of action?
choice_a: Say nothing, since the condition is not visible upon a routine walkthrough
choice_b: Advise the seller to remove all soil before any inspection so the issue cannot be found
choice_c: Disclose it only if a buyer specifically asks whether the yard was ever used for waste disposal
choice_d: Ensure this known material fact is disclosed to prospective buyers, since a licensee generally may not conceal known material facts affecting a property's value or desirability
explanation: Real estate licensees generally have a duty not to conceal known material facts that affect a property's value or desirability, and undisclosed contamination from prior chemical waste disposal is exactly the type of latent material fact that must be disclosed, regardless of whether the buyer thinks to ask about it.
source_note: General real estate license law principles on licensee duty to disclose known material facts

question: Why is completing thorough environmental due diligence (such as a Phase I ESA) especially important for a buyer of commercial or industrial real estate, as opposed to typical single-family residential purchases?
choice_a: Because CERCLA liability can attach to an owner regardless of fault, and commercial/industrial properties carry a higher likelihood of prior contamination from historical operations
choice_b: Because residential buyers are exempt from all environmental laws
choice_c: Because commercial buyers are never eligible for financing without an ESA
choice_d: Because Phase I ESAs are legally required for every real estate transaction nationwide
explanation: Because CERCLA can impose strict liability on a current owner for pre-existing contamination regardless of who caused it, and commercial/industrial sites more often have histories of manufacturing, fuel storage, or chemical use, buyers of such properties have strong incentives to conduct environmental due diligence to assess risk and preserve potential legal defenses.
source_note: CERCLA strict liability framework; industry practice of environmental due diligence in commercial transactions

question: A property is located adjacent to a former industrial site that was placed on the EPA's National Priorities List years ago. A prospective buyer asks the listing agent whether this fact must be disclosed. What is the best response?
choice_a: No disclosure is needed because the contamination is on a neighboring property, not the subject property
choice_b: If the agent has actual knowledge of this material fact and it could reasonably affect the property's value, desirability, or the buyer's willingness to purchase, it should be disclosed
choice_c: Disclosure is prohibited because it could be considered defamatory to the neighboring property owner
choice_d: Only the buyer's attorney can decide whether disclosure is required
explanation: Even when contamination originates on a neighboring parcel, proximity to a known contaminated site (such as an NPL Superfund site) can be a material fact affecting value, marketability, or a buyer's decision to purchase, and known material facts of this kind are generally expected to be disclosed rather than withheld.
source_note: General material fact disclosure principles; EPA National Priorities List

question: Which best describes the general relationship between federal environmental disclosure requirements and state property condition disclosure laws in a typical residential transaction?
choice_a: State disclosure laws are preempted entirely whenever any federal environmental law exists
choice_b: Federal law governs all property disclosures, leaving no role for state law
choice_c: Federal law (such as the lead-based paint disclosure rule) sets specific minimum requirements for certain hazards, while state law separately governs broader seller disclosure obligations for material defects, and both may apply to the same transaction
choice_d: There is no federal disclosure law that applies to residential real estate transactions
explanation: Federal law imposes specific, targeted disclosure duties, most notably for lead-based paint in target housing, while state law typically imposes broader seller property condition disclosure obligations covering material defects generally, including many environmental conditions. Both regimes can and often do apply simultaneously to the same transaction.
source_note: 40 CFR Part 745 (federal lead disclosure); general state seller property condition disclosure statutes

question: A seller fails to provide the required lead-based paint disclosure and EPA pamphlet on the sale of a pre-1978 home. What is a possible consequence under federal law?
choice_a: No consequence exists because the rule is voluntary
choice_b: The buyer automatically forfeits earnest money
choice_c: The transaction is automatically void from inception with no penalty to the seller
choice_d: The seller and any responsible agents can face civil penalties, and the buyer may have grounds to pursue damages or rescind the transaction
explanation: Failure to comply with the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements can expose sellers, lessors, and their agents to civil penalties enforced by EPA/HUD, and can give purchasers a private right of action for damages, potentially including treble damages, in addition to other contract remedies.
source_note: 40 CFR Part 745; Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act enforcement provisions

question: Which of the following is generally true regarding wetlands on a parcel a buyer intends to develop?
choice_a: The presence of jurisdictional wetlands can significantly restrict development and may require a federal permit before any dredging or filling occurs
choice_b: Wetlands designation has no effect on how a property may be developed
choice_c: Wetlands can always be filled without a permit as long as the property is privately owned
choice_d: Only properties larger than 100 acres can contain regulated wetlands
explanation: Land containing jurisdictional wetlands is subject to federal regulation under Clean Water Act Section 404; developing, filling, or dredging such areas without the required Army Corps of Engineers permit can result in significant restrictions, delays, or enforcement action, making wetlands identification an important part of due diligence.
source_note: Clean Water Act Section 404; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers wetlands regulatory program

question: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were banned from most manufacture and use in the United States in 1979 under which federal law, though PCB-containing equipment such as old transformers or fluorescent light ballasts may still be found in older buildings?
choice_a: The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA)
choice_b: The Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA)
choice_c: The Clean Air Act
choice_d: The Safe Drinking Water Act
explanation: TSCA authorized EPA to ban the manufacture, processing, and most uses of PCBs, effective 1979 (with narrow exceptions), due to their toxicity and environmental persistence. Older buildings may still contain legacy PCB-containing equipment, such as transformers, capacitors, or fluorescent light ballasts, manufactured before the ban took effect.
source_note: Toxic Substances Control Act, 15 U.S.C. 2605(e); 40 CFR Part 761 (PCB regulations)

question: A gas station's underground storage tank has leaked gasoline, contaminating the surrounding soil. Which statement about CERCLA's application to this contamination is most accurate?
choice_a: CERCLA automatically imposes strict liability for all petroleum leaks nationwide
choice_b: Only state government may ever respond to a petroleum leak; federal law never applies
choice_c: CERCLA generally excludes petroleum, including gasoline, from its definition of "hazardous substance," so this contamination is typically addressed under RCRA's UST program rather than CERCLA
choice_d: CERCLA requires demolition of any structure located above a petroleum leak
explanation: CERCLA's definition of "hazardous substance" contains a well-known "petroleum exclusion," meaning petroleum and petroleum products, such as the gasoline in this scenario, generally fall outside CERCLA cleanup liability. Leaking petroleum USTs are instead primarily addressed through RCRA Subtitle I's underground storage tank program and related state cleanup programs.
source_note: CERCLA Section 101(14), 42 U.S.C. 9601(14) (petroleum exclusion); RCRA Subtitle I UST program

question: Under federal underground storage tank regulations, which tank is generally EXCLUDED from EPA's UST requirements?
choice_a: A commercial gas station's 10,000-gallon gasoline tank
choice_b: An industrial tank storing regulated hazardous chemicals
choice_c: A newly installed tank at a commercial fueling depot
choice_d: A farm or residential tank of 1,100 gallons or less capacity used to store motor fuel for noncommercial purposes
explanation: EPA's UST regulations under RCRA Subtitle I exclude certain categories of tanks from federal regulation, including farm or residential tanks of 1,100 gallons or less capacity used to store motor fuel for noncommercial purposes, reflecting their comparatively low regulatory priority relative to larger commercial and industrial tanks.
source_note: 40 CFR 280.12 (definition and exclusions for "underground storage tank"); RCRA Subtitle I

question: A contractor is hired to renovate the interior of a home built in 1960, disturbing painted surfaces. Under EPA's Renovation, Repair, and Painting (RRP) Rule, what is generally required?
choice_a: The contractor must be an EPA Lead-Safe Certified firm using lead-safe work practices, since the work disturbs painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing
choice_b: No special certification is required because the RRP Rule applies only to new construction
choice_c: Only a licensed real estate agent may perform or supervise the renovation
choice_d: The RRP Rule applies only to commercial buildings, never to residential housing
explanation: EPA's Renovation, Repair, and Painting Rule requires firms performing renovation, repair, or painting work that disturbs lead-based paint in pre-1978 target housing and child-occupied facilities to be EPA Lead-Safe Certified and to follow specific lead-safe work practices designed to minimize lead dust and debris.
source_note: 40 CFR Part 745, Subpart E (EPA Renovation, Repair, and Painting Rule)

question: The Indoor Radon Abatement Act of 1988 established which national policy goal?
choice_a: That every home be tested for radon before any sale can close
choice_b: That indoor air within buildings in the United States should be as free of radon as the ambient (outdoor) air
choice_c: That radon mitigation systems be installed in every home built before 1978
choice_d: That radon be classified as a hazardous substance under CERCLA
explanation: The Indoor Radon Abatement Act of 1988 declared it a long-term national goal that indoor air be as free of radon as the ambient outdoor air, and directed EPA to develop public information, technical assistance, and voluntary programs to reduce radon exposure; it did not create a mandatory federal pre-sale radon testing requirement.
source_note: Indoor Radon Abatement Act of 1988 (Title III of the Toxic Substances Control Act, 15 U.S.C. 2661 et seq.)

question: EPA's Map of Radon Zones classifies U.S. counties into three zones based on predicted average indoor radon levels. What does a Zone 1 designation indicate?
choice_a: The area has the lowest predicted radon potential, and testing is never advised
choice_b: The designation guarantees that every home in the county will test above the action level
choice_c: The area has the highest predicted average indoor radon screening levels, generally greater than 4 pCi/L
choice_d: Zone 1 applies only to commercial buildings, not residences
explanation: EPA's Map of Radon Zones assigns each U.S. county to Zone 1 (highest potential, predicted average indoor screening levels greater than 4 pCi/L), Zone 2 (moderate potential, 2 to 4 pCi/L), or Zone 3 (low potential, less than 2 pCi/L). The map is a planning tool, and EPA still recommends testing individual homes regardless of zone because radon levels vary house to house.
source_note: EPA Map of Radon Zones; EPA "A Citizen's Guide to Radon"

question: Which transaction is generally EXEMPT from the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements?
choice_a: The sale of a 3-bedroom home built in 1975
choice_b: A long-term lease of a pre-1978 apartment to a family with young children
choice_c: A standard sale of a pre-1978 single-family home to a first-time buyer
choice_d: The sale of housing at foreclosure, or a lease of housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities where no child under age 6 resides or is expected to reside
explanation: The federal lead disclosure rule exempts certain categories of transactions, including sales of housing at foreclosure, short-term leases of 100 days or less with no lease renewal option, leases of housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities (unless a child under age 6 resides or is expected to reside there), and housing already found to be free of lead-based paint, among other narrow exemptions; ordinary sales and leases of pre-1978 housing are not exempt.
source_note: 40 CFR 745.101(c) (exemptions to the federal Lead Disclosure Rule)

question: Under CERCLA Section 107, which of the following is NOT one of the four general categories of "potentially responsible parties" (PRPs) who may be held liable for cleanup costs?
choice_a: A licensed real estate agent who simply listed the property for sale
choice_b: The current owner or operator of the facility
choice_c: The owner or operator at the time hazardous substances were disposed of
choice_d: A person who generated or arranged for disposal of hazardous substances sent to the facility
explanation: CERCLA identifies four categories of potentially responsible parties: (1) current owners/operators, (2) owners/operators at the time of disposal, (3) generators or arrangers of hazardous substances disposed of at the facility, and (4) transporters who selected the disposal site. A real estate agent who merely lists or markets a property is not, by virtue of that role, a PRP under CERCLA.
source_note: CERCLA Section 107(a), 42 U.S.C. 9607(a)

question: A buyer conducted a Phase I ESA before purchasing a contaminated commercial site and qualified as a "bona fide prospective purchaser" under CERCLA. To retain this liability protection after closing, the buyer must generally continue to do which of the following?
choice_a: Nothing further; the protection is fully secured once the pre-purchase Phase I ESA is complete
choice_b: Exercise appropriate care with respect to any hazardous substances, comply with land use restrictions, and cooperate with parties conducting response actions at the site
choice_c: Immediately resell the property to avoid any ongoing obligations
choice_d: File suit against the prior owner within 30 days of closing
explanation: Qualifying as a bona fide prospective purchaser under CERCLA is not a one-time, pre-closing event; it requires ongoing compliance after acquisition, including exercising appropriate care to stop continuing releases, complying with land use restrictions and institutional controls, providing full cooperation and access to persons performing response actions, and complying with information requests.
source_note: CERCLA Section 101(40), 42 U.S.C. 9601(40) (bona fide prospective purchaser continuing obligations)

question: Besides providing liability relief for qualifying purchasers, how does federal brownfields policy further encourage redevelopment of contaminated or potentially contaminated sites?
choice_a: By automatically transferring ownership of brownfield sites to the federal government
choice_b: By banning any future development on brownfield sites
choice_c: Through EPA grant and loan programs that help fund environmental assessment and cleanup of brownfield sites
choice_d: By requiring brownfield sites to remain vacant for a minimum of 50 years
explanation: In addition to liability protections for bona fide prospective purchasers, the federal brownfields program, administered by EPA under the Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act of 2002, provides competitive grants and loans to states, tribes, and local governments to assess and clean up brownfield sites, encouraging their productive redevelopment and reuse.
source_note: Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act of 2002; EPA Brownfields Program grants

question: In a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, a "Recognized Environmental Condition" (REC) refers to:
choice_a: Any cosmetic damage to a building's exterior finish
choice_b: A zoning violation unrelated to environmental contamination
choice_c: The existence of a homeowners association restriction
choice_d: The presence or likely presence of hazardous substances or petroleum products on a property due to a release, under conditions indicative of a release, or under conditions creating a material threat of a future release
explanation: ASTM E1527 defines a "recognized environmental condition" as the presence or likely presence of hazardous substances or petroleum products in, on, or at a property due to a release to the environment, under conditions indicative of a release, or under conditions that pose a material threat of a future release. Identifying a REC in a Phase I ESA typically leads to a recommendation for a Phase II ESA.
source_note: ASTM E1527 Standard Practice for Phase I Environmental Site Assessments

question: Which Clean Water Act permit program regulates direct discharges of pollutants from point sources, such as a pipe or ditch, into waters of the United States, as distinguished from the dredge-and-fill permitting used for wetlands?
choice_a: The National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) under Section 402
choice_b: The Section 404 dredge-and-fill permit program
choice_c: The National Flood Insurance Program
choice_d: The federal Underground Storage Tank program
explanation: Section 402 of the Clean Water Act establishes the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which requires permits for the discharge of pollutants from point sources, such as pipes or ditches, into waters of the United States. This is distinct from the Section 404 program, which governs the discharge of dredged or fill material and is most relevant to wetlands.
source_note: Clean Water Act Section 402, 33 U.S.C. 1342 (NPDES permit program)

question: The Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (EPCRA), added by Title III of SARA, primarily requires:
choice_a: Sellers to test residential wells for contamination before every closing
choice_b: Certain facilities to report hazardous chemical inventories and releases, feeding data into the publicly available Toxics Release Inventory (TRI)
choice_c: All real estate licensees to complete environmental law continuing education
choice_d: Automatic condemnation of any property located near a reporting facility
explanation: EPCRA requires facilities that manufacture, store, or use certain hazardous chemicals above threshold quantities to report inventories and releases to state and local emergency planning authorities, and to submit data used to compile EPA's Toxics Release Inventory, giving communities and prospective property buyers a public source of information about nearby chemical hazards.
source_note: Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act of 1986 (SARA Title III); EPA Toxics Release Inventory (TRI)

question: Concerns about formaldehyde off-gassing from particleboard, medium-density fiberboard, and hardwood plywood used in home construction and cabinetry are addressed at the federal level by which law?
choice_a: The Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act
choice_b: The National Flood Insurance Act
choice_c: The Formaldehyde Standards for Composite Wood Products Act, added as Title VI to the Toxic Substances Control Act
choice_d: RCRA Subtitle I
explanation: The Formaldehyde Standards for Composite Wood Products Act, enacted in 2010 and added as Title VI to TSCA, directs EPA to regulate formaldehyde emissions from composite wood products such as particleboard, medium-density fiberboard, and hardwood plywood, which are common sources of indoor formaldehyde exposure in newer construction and cabinetry.
source_note: Formaldehyde Standards for Composite Wood Products Act (TSCA Title VI, 15 U.S.C. 2697); 40 CFR Part 770

question: In Sackett v. EPA (2023), the U.S. Supreme Court narrowed federal jurisdiction over wetlands under the Clean Water Act by holding that wetlands qualify as "waters of the United States" only when they:
choice_a: Are located within 500 feet of any body of water
choice_b: Are designated as wetlands on a county zoning map
choice_c: Contain any standing water at any time of year
choice_d: Have a continuous surface connection to a relatively permanent body of water that is itself a water of the United States
explanation: In Sackett v. EPA, 598 U.S. 651 (2023), the Supreme Court held that wetlands fall under Clean Water Act jurisdiction only if they have a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water that are themselves waters of the United States, narrowing the broader "significant nexus" standard some lower courts had previously applied and reducing the scope of federally regulated wetlands.
source_note: Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency, 598 U.S. 651 (2023)

question: A facility stores oil in large aboveground storage tanks (ASTs) near a river. Which federal program is most directly aimed at preventing oil discharges from such tanks into navigable waters?
choice_a: The Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule under the Clean Water Act
choice_b: The RCRA Subtitle I underground storage tank program
choice_c: The federal lead-based paint disclosure rule
choice_d: The National Flood Insurance Program
explanation: While underground storage tanks are regulated under RCRA Subtitle I, aboveground storage tanks storing oil above certain threshold quantities are instead subject to the Clean Water Act's Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule, which requires facilities to prepare spill prevention plans and implement secondary containment measures to prevent oil discharges into navigable waters.
source_note: Clean Water Act; 40 CFR Part 112 (SPCC Rule)

question: A landowner's property becomes contaminated solely because hazardous substances migrated through groundwater from a neighboring, contiguous industrial site, with no act or omission by the landowner contributing to the contamination. Which CERCLA liability protection is most relevant here?
choice_a: The bona fide prospective purchaser defense, which applies only to buyers who knowingly acquire already-contaminated property
choice_b: The contiguous property owner defense, which can protect an owner whose land is contaminated solely by a release migrating from a contiguous or similarly situated property, provided the owner did not cause the contamination and exercises appropriate care
choice_c: The innocent landowner defense, which applies only to a purchaser who did not know of contamination at the time of acquiring the contaminated parcel itself
choice_d: There is no CERCLA defense available in this situation
explanation: The 2002 Brownfields amendments to CERCLA created a distinct contiguous property owner defense, protecting landowners whose property becomes contaminated solely as a result of a release from a contiguous or similarly situated property, so long as the owner did not cause or contribute to the contamination, exercises appropriate care, and meets other statutory conditions. This is a separate protection from the innocent landowner and bona fide prospective purchaser defenses, both of which involve the landowner's own acquisition of the contaminated parcel.
source_note: CERCLA Section 107(q), 42 U.S.C. 9607(q); Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act of 2002
